svg.text: The 23 GoF patterns, mapped by the one question that picks them — what is going to change?

Every box gives the pattern name, then the axis it isolates in the book's own wording, then the single thing worth remembering about it. Read the three bands top to bottom: objects get MADE, objects get COMBINED, responsibility FLOWS.
The arrows are the relationships between patterns — what is built from what, what is an alternative to what, and which pairs are confused so often that the confusion is worth drawing.
1 · OBJECTS GET MADE DIFFERENTLY · creational, 5 patterns · every one of them exists to remove a hard-coded `new` from code that should not care about concrete types
2 · OBJECTS GET COMBINED DIFFERENTLY · structural, 7 patterns · five of the seven are wrappers; what separates them is never the shape, it is the INTENT
3 · RESPONSIBILITY FLOWS DIFFERENTLY · behavioural, 11 patterns · the largest group, because the hard question is not what the objects are but who is responsible and how control reaches them
4 · WHAT THE CATALOGUE ACTUALLY TEACHES · not patterns, but the four things that decide whether any of them helps you

Factory Method · Adapter (class form) · Template Method · Interpreter.
Their variation point is an overridden method, so it is frozen the moment
you pick a subclass. The other nineteen compose objects, so they can still
change while the program runs. Four against nineteen is the book voting.
Abstract Factory: a new FAMILY is cheap, a new PRODUCT is expensive.
Visitor: a new OPERATION is cheap, a new NODE TYPE is expensive.
Both invert normal OO extensibility, and both will fight you every sprint
if you guessed wrong. Ask which axis moves BEFORE adopting either.
MVC is not one of the 23
The book analyses it in the introduction as a COMPOUND: Observer for
view updates, Composite for nested views, Strategy for the controller.
It is deliberately absent from the catalogue — which is precisely why no
two teams have ever agreed on what MVC means.
The two sentences it all rests on
1. Program to an interface, not an implementation.
2. Favour object composition over class inheritance.
Inheritance is white-box reuse: static, and it leaks the parent's internals
into the child. Composition is black-box, paid for in extra plumbing.

Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software — Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides (Addison-Wesley, 1994). The “varies” wording follows the book's own Table 1.2. Companion to the 24 runnable Java files in this folder.
